newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: New management key to South Korea Jinro's survival.
newsitem.headline: New management key to South Korea Jinro's survival.

text.p: South Korea's troubled Jinro Group won a small reprieve on Tuesday when one creditor extended debt payments for a key affiliate, but analysts said the group would ultimately fail unless it gave creditors management control.

"The Jinro Group does not seem to realise the seriousness of its problems. It has no choice but to give up managerial rights if it wants to survive," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
"Without strong support from creditor banks and without more intensive self-rescue efforts, it will be difficult for the group to survive," Rhee said.
The group's distiller flagship Jinro Ltd on Monday defaulted on repayments of about eight billion won ($8.97 million) worth of promissory notes.
The holder of those notes, Donghwa Leasing Co Ltd, said on Tuesday it would extend the repayment to next February.
If Donghwa had not agreed to the extension and Jinro had failed to meet the second deadline on Tuesday, it would have triggered court-receivership proceedings.
"We have decided to extend repayment of Jinro's loans because of worries about the adverse impacts the default would have on the nation's economy," said a Donghwa official.
But analysts said Donghwa's extension was far from a solution to Jinro's problems.
The Jinro Group, the nation's 19th largest business conglomerate, buckled in April under 3.2 trillion won in debt, mostly a result of overly ambitious expansion.
Jinro then became the first conglomerate to benefit from a committee of banks formed to keep troubled corporates afloat.
The committee protected Jinro for two months, and on July 25 agreed to extend 36.9 billion won to Jinro on the condition that the company turn over its managerial rights to creditors.
But Jinro has not complied with that condition and the new loans have not been provided.
Jinro's creditor banks on Tuesday again urged Jinro to give up its managerial rights in exchange for emergency loans. But Jinro turned down the offer and said it would seek a reprieve from Donghwa.

"An improvement in cash appears to have made the Jinro management bold. But loan repayment requirements will continue to haunt the group," said Hwang Chan, an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.

Earlier in July, the group said it would sell 12 of its 18 affiliates and some real estate in an effort to raise over 840 billion won by the end of this year to rescue six companies set for bailout by the bank committee.
Shares of the Jinro Group's two listed firms dropped by their daily limit on news of the default.
Jinro Ind. fell 400 won to its daily lower limit of 4,620, while Jinro General Foods dropped 300 won to its limit of 3,560.
Trading of Jinro Ltd was suspended for Tuesday because of the default.
Seoul stocks closed at 732.68, off 1.24 points, as Jinro's difficulties kept investors away.
"The Jinro trouble was definitely bad news. But investors refrained from dumping shares because of the view the market was oversold," said Park Young-shik of Daewoo Securities.
